procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but the case likely originated with a grievance that the appellants wanted investigated, leading to the filing of a writ petition.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 10.05.2023 passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Chhattisgarh in W.P.Cr. No.197 of 2016.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellants filed a writ petition (W.P. Crl. No. 197 of 2016) under Article 226 of the Constitution of India in the High Court of Chhattisgarh, seeking writs of mandamus and certiorari. The High Court dismissed the petition on 10.05.2023, stating that the appellants had an adequate statutory remedy available under section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. by approaching the Magistrate concerned. The petition remained pending for about seven years.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants appealed the High Court's order to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 3738 of 2024).

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside.
The CBI-respondent no. 8 is directed to carry out complete and fair investigation and proceed in accordance to law into the incident expeditiously and submit a report to this Court.
If the CBI finds that an FIR needs to be registered, it may itself do so and proceed accordingly and bring such complaint to a logical conclusion.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition seeking a CBI investigation on the ground that an alternative statutory remedy under Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. was available.

facts: The appellants (mother and brother of the deceased) sought a CBI investigation into the suspicious death of the wife of a senior judicial officer.
They alleged that the husband had influenced the state police, preventing an FIR from being registered and ensuring no fair investigation was conducted.

The High Court dismissed their writ petition, which had been pending for seven years, on the grounds that they had an alternative statutory remedy by approaching a Magistrate under Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C.
law: The power of a constitutional court to direct a CBI investigation should be exercised sparingly and not in a routine manner.

However, this power can be used to ensure complete justice and to enforce the fundamental right to a fair investigation, especially when there are allegations of bias or undue influence on the state's police machinery.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged the appellants' argument that approaching a Magistrate under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. would be futile, as the Magistrate would be an officer subordinate to the husband, who is a senior judicial officer.
The Court found that the husband's position as a senior judicial officer created a reasonable apprehension of bias and undue influence on the state police.

Given these specific circumstances, the Court determined that an investigation by an independent agency like the CBI was necessary to dispel any doubts, ensure a fair and thorough investigation, and ultimately do complete justice for the appellants.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in dismissing the writ petition. The special circumstances of the case, particularly the involvement of a senior judicial officer and the resulting apprehension of bias, made the alternative remedy under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. inadequate. Therefore, to enforce the fundamental right to a fair investigation, the Court set aside the High Court's order and directed the CBI to conduct a complete investigation.

issue.issue_text: Whether an investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is warranted considering the allegations of bias and undue influence on the state police machinery, particularly when the husband of the deceased is a senior judicial officer.

facts: The case involves the suspicious death of a woman whose husband is a senior judicial officer in Chhattisgarh.
The deceased's family (appellants) alleged that the death was not a simple suicide and that the husband, due to his position, had influenced the state police and the post-mortem report.
The appellants claimed that despite their complaints, no FIR was registered and a fair investigation was not conducted by the state police.
The High Court had previously dismissed the appellants' petition, stating they had an alternative statutory remedy available.
law: The power to direct a CBI investigation is an extraordinary power that must be exercised sparingly, cautiously, and only in exceptional situations.
Such an order should not be passed routinely or merely because allegations are made against the local police.

A CBI investigation may be ordered when it is necessary to provide credibility, instill confidence in the investigation, do complete justice, and enforce the fundamental right to a fair investigation.
application: The Court acknowledged the general rule that ordering a CBI probe should be rare.
However, it found this case to be exceptional due to the specific facts. The primary consideration was that the husband of the deceased is a senior judicial officer.
This status, combined with the family's allegations of bias and undue influence on the state police, created a situation where any doubt or apprehension needed to be dispelled.
The Court reasoned that to ensure a thorough, fair, and independent investigation and to uncover the truth about the incident (particularly the ante-mortem injuries), a CBI probe was necessary.
Handing the case to the CBI would do complete justice, enforce the family's fundamental right to a fair investigation, and instill confidence in the outcome.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a CBI investigation was warranted. It set aside the High Court's order and directed the CBI to conduct a complete, fair, and expeditious investigation into the suspicious death to remove any doubts and ensure justice, given the unique circumstance of the husband's position as a senior judicial officer.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition seeking a CBI investigation on the ground that an alternative statutory remedy under Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. was available.
appellant_arguments: While the remedy under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. exists, it is not a viable or effective remedy in this specific case.
Respondent no. 7 is a senior judicial officer, and a Magistrate, being a subordinate officer, would be under his influence, offering no hope of getting justice.
These exceptional circumstances justified approaching the High Court directly under Article 226 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The appellants should be left at liberty to approach the Magistrate under the available statutory remedy of Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is warranted considering the allegations of bias and undue influence on the state police machinery, particularly when the husband of the deceased is a senior judicial officer.
appellant_arguments: Respondent no. 7, a senior judicial officer, has already exercised his influence on the administration to ensure that an FIR is not registered.
Due to the respondent's influence, no free and fair investigation can be carried out by the state police machinery.
respondent_arguments: The state police conducted a detailed and thorough inquiry, recording statements of more than 50 witnesses, and found no evidence against respondent no. 7.
The appellants are unnecessarily doubting the credibility of the entire state police machinery of Chhattisgarh.
Respondent no. 7 is a judicial officer with a good reputation who is being unnecessarily targeted by the appellants for ulterior motives.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The extraordinary power to direct a CBI investigation must be exercised sparingly, cautiously, and in exceptional situations where it is necessary to provide credibility and instill confidence in the investigation.
obiter: Regardless of the motive for a murder, it is the responsibility of the police to conduct a thorough investigation, as any slackness in the process is not in the public interest.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Considering that the respondent is a senior judicial officer, any doubt or apprehension in the minds of the appellants, who have lost a family member, must be dispelled by an investigation carried out by the CBI. This is necessary to do complete justice and enforce the fundamental right to a fair investigation, which in this exceptional situation, requires an independent agency to instill confidence and credibility.
legal_tests_applied: The extraordinary power to direct a CBI investigation must be exercised sparingly, cautiously, and in exceptional situations where it becomes necessary to provide credibility and instil confidence in investigations, or where such an order may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing fundamental rights.
policy_considerations: Unresolved crimes tend to erode public trust in institutions which have been established for maintaining law and order.
It is the responsibility of the police to come up to the expectation of the public at large and display that no stone will remain unturned to book the culprits.
Courts need to be alive to genuine grievances brought before it by ordinary citizens.

It is our responsibility to ensure that the prosecution agency is reminded of its responsibility and duties in the discharge of its functions effectively and efficiently and ensure that the criminal prosecution is carried on effectively and the perpetrators of crime are duly punished by the appropriate court of law.
